paragraphs.title: A Cry and a Request for a Clear Judgment

easy.explanation: Job says, “My soul is weary of my life.”
Job says he will speak “in the bitterness of my soul.”
easy.q: What does Job want to express?

easy.explanation: Job says, “I will say unto God.”
easy.q: To whom does Job turn with his request?

answers: So he can understand the charge against him
So he can praise his friends
So he can leave his country
medium.explanation: Job asks God to explain the reason for his suffering.
medium.q: Why does Job ask God to show him wherefore He contends with him?

answers: Job is deeply tired of living
medium.explanation: The phrase expresses Job’s profound distress and weariness.
medium.q: What does the phrase “weary of my life” communicate?

answers: Job expresses bitterness and then asks God for an explanation
Job praises God and then thanks Him
Job describes his birth and then his death
medium.explanation: Job first describes his inward anguish and then directly asks God about his situation.
medium.q: What movement occurs between verses 1 and 2?

answers: That God give him a clear explanation
challenge.explanation: Job asks God to show him why He is contending with him.
challenge.q: What central request does Job make?

answers: He turns his pain into a demand for justice and explanation
challenge.explanation: Job brings his personal bitterness directly before God.
challenge.q: What does Job’s direct address to God reveal?

answers: He suffers, yet he still appeals to God for an answer
He is joyful, yet asks for punishment
He praises his friends while denying his own words
challenge.explanation: Although Job is bitter and distressed, he continues speaking directly to God.
challenge.q: What tension appears in Job’s words?

short_answers.question: What is Job weary of?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “My soul is weary of my life.”

short_answers.question: In what spirit will Job speak?
short_answers.answer: In the bitterness of his soul.
short_answers.explanation: Job explicitly uses this phrase in verse 1.

short_answers.question: What does Job ask God to show him?
short_answers.explanation: Job asks, “shew me wherefore thou contendest with me.”

paragraphs.title: Questions of Justice and Divine Knowledge

answers: Why He oppresses and despises it
easy.explanation: Job asks whether it is good for God to oppress and despise the work of His hands.
easy.q: What does Job ask God about His treatment of His work?

easy.explanation: Job asks why God shines upon “the counsel of the wicked.”
easy.q: Whose counsel does Job say God appears to shine upon?

answers: God is not limited by human sight or human days
easy.explanation: Job asks whether God has eyes of flesh and whether His years are like man’s days.
easy.q: How does God differ from man in verses 4–5?

medium.explanation: To oppress is to afflict or deal harshly with someone.
medium.q: What does “oppress” mean in this passage?

answers: To emphasize God’s knowledge beyond human sight
To say that God cannot see
medium.explanation: Job contrasts divine knowledge with the limited sight of human beings.
medium.q: Why does Job mention that God does not see as man sees?

answers: A question about justice, a description of divine knowledge, and a question about searching out sin
A description of birth, a description of the body, and a request for rest
Praise of the wicked, confession of sin, and a prayer
medium.explanation: Job begins by questioning God’s treatment of His creation and ends by asking why God searches out his sin.

answers: That God knows all things and still searches for his sin
challenge.explanation: Job emphasizes God’s knowledge while struggling to understand why God still examines him for iniquity.
challenge.q: What troubles Job most about God’s knowledge?

answers: Job questions the justice of God’s treatment of him
Job wants to become a creator
challenge.explanation: Job finds it difficult to understand why the Creator would oppress His creation.
challenge.q: What is implied by Job’s question about God oppressing His own work?

answers: No one can rescue Job from God’s hand
God has no interest in Job
challenge.explanation: Job acknowledges that no one can deliver him from God’s power.
challenge.q: What does “there is none that can deliver out of thine hand” mean?

short_answers.question: Whose counsel does Job say God shines upon?
Does Job say God’s days are like man’s days?
short_answers.explanation: Job asks whether God’s days and years are like man’s, implying that they are not.

short_answers.question: Who can deliver Job out of God’s hand?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “there is none that can deliver out of thine hand.”

paragraphs.title: The Creator Who Turns Against His Creation

easy.explanation: Job says, “Thine hands have made me and fashioned me.”
easy.q: What does Job say God’s hands have done?

easy.explanation: Job describes being clothed with skin and flesh and fenced with bones and sinews.
easy.q: What parts of the human body are mentioned in verses 10–11?

easy.explanation: Job says, “Thou hast granted me life and favour.”
easy.q: What did God grant Job according to verse 12?

answers: God is the Creator and giver of life, yet Job feels that He is destroying him
God is both a man and a wicked person
God is distant and knows nothing
medium.explanation: Job remembers God’s creative and gracious work while also describing his present destruction.

answers: Kept or held in secret knowledge
medium.explanation: Job says that these matters were hidden or kept in God’s heart.
medium.q: What does “hid in thine heart” mean in context?

answers: From clay to the forming of the body covered with skin and flesh
medium.explanation: The description moves from clay to the formation and covering of the human body.
medium.q: How does Job’s description develop in verses 9–11?

answers: It reminds him that God has known and formed him from the beginning
It proves that Job is not human
It shows that the body is unimportant
challenge.explanation: Job appeals to the close relationship between the Creator and His creation.
challenge.q: Why does Job mention the making of his body?

answers: Job recognizes that his life was given and sustained by God’s kindness
Job claims that his spirit does not exist
challenge.explanation: Job acknowledges God’s gift of life and His preservation of his spirit.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the combination of “life and favour” and the preservation of Job’s spirit?

answers: God does not know his thoughts
God knows the things hidden in the heart
challenge.explanation: Job says, “these things hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this is with thee.”
challenge.q: What does Job emphasize at the end of the passage?

short_answers.question: What did God grant Job?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “Thou hast granted me life and favour.”

short_answers.question: With what did God make Job?
short_answers.explanation: Job asks God to remember that He made him as the clay.

short_answers.question: What preserved Job’s spirit?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “thy visitation hath preserved my spirit.”

paragraphs.title: No Escape Between Guilt and Innocence

easy.explanation: Job says, “If I sin, then thou markest me.”

answers: He can freely lift up his head
He still cannot lift up his head
He does not suffer at all
easy.explanation: Job says, “if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head.”
easy.q: How does Job feel even if he is righteous?

easy.explanation: Job says, “Thou huntest me as a fierce lion.”
easy.q: To what does Job compare being hunted?

medium.explanation: Job describes himself as overwhelmed by confusion, disgrace, and affliction.

answers: In both cases he feels he has no rest or honor
In both cases he becomes wealthy
In both cases he escapes from God
medium.explanation: Whether wicked or righteous, Job feels unable to escape humiliation and suffering.
medium.q: What do the conditions of sin and righteousness have in common for Job?

answers: Witnesses and indignation are repeatedly brought against him
medium.explanation: Job says that God renews His witnesses and increases His indignation against him.
medium.q: How do the troubles increase in verse 17?

answers: Every condition seems to lead him to disgrace
Job is certain of his victory
God has no interest in him
challenge.explanation: Job feels trapped: sin brings accusation, while righteousness still brings humiliation.
challenge.q: What central feeling is expressed by Job’s situation?

answers: It emphasizes Job’s sense of being hunted and pursued
It proves Job was a hunter
challenge.explanation: The lion image presents Job as prey being relentlessly pursued.
challenge.q: What does the image of the fierce lion add to the passage?

answers: Job feels that accusations and sufferings are accumulating
Job asks to enter a battle
challenge.explanation: These terms create an image of mounting pressure and conflict against Job.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the language of witnesses, indignation, changes, and war?

short_answers.question: What does God do if Job sins?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “If I sin, then thou markest me.”

short_answers.question: What is Job full of?
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “I am full of confusion.”

short_answers.question: How does Job say God hunts him?

paragraphs.title: The Wish for Death and the Land of Darkness

answers: That he was brought forth from the womb
That he was not made king
That he did not receive wealth
easy.explanation: Job asks why God brought him forth out of the womb.
easy.q: What does Job regret in verse 18?

easy.explanation: Job says he should have been carried from the womb to the grave.
easy.q: Where would Job rather have gone from the womb?

answers: A land of light and joy
A land of water and flowers
A land of darkness and the shadow of death
easy.explanation: Job describes it as a land of darkness and the shadow of death.
easy.q: How is the land Job describes characterized?

medium.explanation: Job asks God to let him alone so that he may take comfort a little.
medium.q: What does Job ask for before he dies?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the grave or underworld as a place of deep darkness.
medium.q: What does “the land of darkness” suggest?

answers: Regret over birth, a request for rest, and a description of the land of darkness
Praise for life, a request for wealth, and a description of a garden
Confession of sin, a prayer for victory, and a description of a city
medium.explanation: Job moves from regret over being born to a request for brief rest and then describes the dark land.

answers: The depth of his despair over life
challenge.explanation: Job’s wish that he had gone from the womb to the grave shows his profound despair.
challenge.q: What does Job’s preference for the grave reveal?

answers: The land has no order or brightness
challenge.explanation: Job portrays the place of darkness as lacking order and clarity.
challenge.q: What is suggested by “without any order”?

answers: As light that does not exist at all
As light that is like darkness
challenge.explanation: Job says that in this land “the light is as darkness.”
challenge.q: How is the light described in the land of darkness?

short_answers.question: Where would Job rather have been carried?
short_answers.answer: From the womb to the grave.
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “I should have been carried from the womb to the grave.”

short_answers.question: What does Job ask God to let him do?
short_answers.explanation: Job asks to be left alone so that he may take comfort briefly.

short_answers.question: What is the light like in the land of darkness?
short_answers.explanation: The final verse says, “where the light is as darkness.”
